difficulty.rationale: The examinee must discriminate an atypical parkinsonian syndrome from idiopathic Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, corticobasal syndrome, and dementia with Lewy bodies using the pattern of early backward falls, axial rigidity, poor levodopa response, and vertical supranuclear gaze impairment.

duplicate_gate.selector_alignment_note: Ramsay Hunt syndrome was not selected because the official outline places it under Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue, not this selector system.
duplicate_gate.selected_construct: Progressive supranuclear palsy presenting with early postural instability/backward falls, axial rigidity, and vertical supranuclear gaze palsy

option_audit.progressive_supranuclear_palsy: Uniquely integrates early backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity with extended posture, poor levodopa response, minimal resting tremor, and vertical supranuclear gaze dysfunction.
option_audit.idiopathic_Parkinson_disease: Bradykinesia and rigidity overlap, but early backward falls, axial extension, vertical supranuclear gaze impairment and poor levodopa response are red flags against typical Parkinson disease.
option_audit.multiple_system_atrophy: Poor levodopa response can overlap, but MSA is more strongly associated with prominent autonomic failure and/or cerebellar features; the presented vertical gaze plus early backward-fall pattern is more characteristic of PSP.
option_audit.corticobasal_syndrome: Can produce atypical parkinsonism, but the classic syndrome is asymmetric and limb-predominant with cortical features such as apraxia, cortical sensory loss, myoclonus/dystonia, or alien-limb phenomenon.
option_audit.dementia_with_Lewy_bodies: Can produce parkinsonism and falls, but requires an early dementia syndrome with characteristic fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations and often REM sleep behavior disorder; these are absent.

adversarial_second_pass.independent_reconstruction: An older adult develops symmetric akinetic-rigid parkinsonism, backward falls within the first year, axial/neck rigidity with extended posture, poor levodopa response, and slowed/limited vertical eye movements with relatively preserved horizontal movements. This reconstructs PSP without relying on the answer choices.
adversarial_second_pass.Parkinson_disease_attack: Typical Parkinson disease could explain bradykinesia and rigidity but not this cluster of early backward falls, vertical supranuclear gaze dysfunction, axial extension and poor levodopa response as well as PSP does.
adversarial_second_pass.MSA_attack: MSA is a valid atypical-parkinsonism distractor and may be levodopa-poor, but the vignette supplies no dysautonomia or cerebellar syndrome and does supply a classic PSP ocular-postural signature.
adversarial_second_pass.CBS_attack: CBS is a close tauopathy differential, but the absence of asymmetric limb-predominant cortical signs plus the presence of vertical gaze dysfunction and early backward falls make PSP uniquely better.
adversarial_second_pass.DLB_attack: DLB shares parkinsonism and may cause falls, but no early cognitive decline, fluctuations, hallucinations, or REM-sleep-behavior clues are present.
adversarial_second_pass.cueing_check: The correct option is not lexically embedded in the stem; no acronym or disease-specific eponym is given.
adversarial_second_pass.unsupported_precision_check: The vignette uses a 2-year history and first-year falls because first-year falls are directly incorporated in classic PSP diagnostic criteria/supporting descriptions. It does not assert numerical imaging cutoffs, prognostic duration, treatment dose, or response percentage.
adversarial_second_pass.source_currentness_correction: A generic-date NIA DLB source was replaced with a dated NCBI/StatPearls source before finalization, followed by a fresh successful canonical duplicate scan.
